questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes cognitive analytic therapy?

options.text: It is based on conflicts and role disturbances seen in the immediate environment
It is built on a hierarchy of goals
Hypothesis testing is carried out by the patient as homework
It is a structured therapy focused on cognitive and emotional functioning along with reformulation

correct_answer.text: It is a structured therapy focused on cognitive and emotional functioning along with reformulation

correct_answers.text: It is a structured therapy focused on cognitive and emotional functioning along with reformulation

questions.explanation: Cognitive analytic therapy (CAT) is a therapy method introduced by Anthony Ryle in 1990. It aims to bring together ideas from dynamic, cognitive, and behavioural therapies by attempting to explain psychoanalytic ideas in cognitive terms. The 'three Rs' of CAT are the recognition of maladaptive behaviour and beliefs, reformulation of these (the main 'work' of therapy), and revision. The reformulation is agreed between the therapist and patient and documented in a 'psychotherapy file'. This reformulation is expressed in narrative and diagrammatic forms and considers both the past history and current problems. It is used throughout therapy to guide the active focus, to set homework, and to enable recognition of transference/countertransference. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 918.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is correct about dialectical behaviour therapy?

options.text: It is only done in groups
It is built on a hierarchy of goals
Low frustration tolerance is a contraindication
It is based on psychodynamic formulations

correct_answer.text: It is built on a hierarchy of goals

correct_answers.text: It is built on a hierarchy of goals

questions.explanation: Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) was introduced in 1991 by Linehan and colleagues as a treatment for borderline personality disorder (BPD). Patients with BPD are supported in understanding their own emotional experiences and are taught new skills for dealing with their distress through a combination of group and individual therapy sessions. DBT is a complex treatment combining CBT interventions with Eastern meditative practice, notably mindfulness. DBT takes a hierarchical view of treatment aspirations, with the focus first on reducing behaviours that cause self-harm, then on reducing those behaviours that interfere with therapy, and finally aiming to reduce behaviours that diminish the quality of life and personal relationships. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 916-917.

questions.question_text: In multisystemic therapy, treatment is usually given for a period of
questions.explanation: Multisystemic therapy (MST) is one the most established treatments for conduct disorder. MST targets antisocial behaviours and is delivered in the day-to-day environment (such as home or school) by a treatment team consisting of a therapist, case manager, and behavioural management specialist, typically over 3-5 months. This intervention is particularly intensive, with closely supervised therapists who have low caseloads to allow for multiple weekly contacts and on-call support 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Ref: Fairchild G et al. Conduct disorder. Nature Reviews Disease Primers. 2019 Jun 27;5(1):43.

questions.question_text: The target age range for functional family therapy in the treatment of conduct disorder is
questions.explanation: Functional family therapy (FFT) is a family-based intervention that was designed to increase family problem-solving skills, emotional cohesion, and related parenting skills in families of young people aged 11-18 with one or more of the following problems: delinquency, violence, antisocial behaviour, substance abuse, conduct disorder, oppositional defiant disorder, or disruptive behaviour disorders. FFT is generally delivered over a 3-month period. Ref: Fairchild G et al. Conduct disorder. Nature Reviews Disease Primers. 2019 Jun 27;5(1):43. Littell JH et al. Functional Family Therapy for families of youth (age 11-18) with behaviour problems. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017 Jan;2017(1).

questions.question_text: Cognitive analytic therapy usually lasts for how many sessions?
questions.explanation: Cognitive analytic therapy (CAT) is a therapy method introduced by Anthony Ryle in 1990. It aims to bring together ideas from dynamic, cognitive, and behavioural therapies by attempting to explain psychoanalytic ideas in cognitive terms. It consists of 8-24 sessions, normally 12. There may be a planned 3-month review appointment after therapy has ended. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 918-919.

questions.question_text: A psychotherapist makes a practical link between the patient's mental symptoms and disturbing life events that either trigger or follow from the onset of the symptoms. She also defines the problem as a medical illness and gives the patient the sick role. Which of the following patients is most likely to find this approach useful?

options.text: A 55 year old man convicted for multiple sexual offences
A 14 year old boy with conduct disorder
A 16 year old girl with bulimia nervosa
A 66 year old woman with psychotic depression
A 45 year old man with cocaine use disorder

correct_answer.text: A 16 year old girl with bulimia nervosa

correct_answers.text: A 16 year old girl with bulimia nervosa

questions.explanation: Interpersonal therapy (IPT) was developed in the 1970s by Klerman and Weissman as a treatment for depressive illness, and later developed for use in other disorders. Illnesses are viewed as medical disorders, diagnosed according to standard criteria, and rated in severity by rating scales. A key feature of IPT involves 'giving the sick role' to the patient. The main indication for IPT is non-psychotic depressive disorders. Adaptations of IPT have been applied to various subgroups such as adolescents, geriatric patients, primary care clinic patients, and patients with HIV, bulimia, panic disorder, bipolar disorder, dysthymic disorder, bereavement, postpartum depression, social phobia, and insomnia. IPT is not indicated for substance abuse or personality disorders. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 914-915.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is incorrect with respect to the principles of psychodynamic psychotherapy?

options.text: Analysis of the transference is the only means to access the unconscious mind
A therapist gains insight into the client's issues by interpreting unconscious motives
Worsening of symptoms is not uncommon during the course of therapy
Humans are instinctively irrational and destructive
Object loss can be associated with manic states

correct_answer.text: Analysis of the transference is the only means to access the unconscious mind

correct_answers.text: Analysis of the transference is the only means to access the unconscious mind

questions.explanation: Psychodynamic psychotherapy is an intervention where the concepts of symptom development are based on those of psychoanalysis, but the methods of therapy are adjusted for a reduced frequency of sessions and decreased number of total sessions. An unconscious mind is believed to affect one's perceptions and actions. Traditional techniques to attempt to interpret unconscious content include the 'fundamental rule' of free association, analysis of the transference/countertransference, the interpretation of dreams and 'parapraxes', and the symbolism of neurotic symptoms. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 898-902.

questions.question_text: Interpersonal therapy was developed by
questions.explanation: Interpersonal therapy (IPT) was developed in the 1970s by Klerman and Weissman as a treatment for depressive illness, and later developed for use in other disorders. IPT is a practical, short-term therapy (12-16 hour-long sessions) that aims, by improving interpersonal functioning, to improve emotional symptoms. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 914-915.

questions.question_text: At the second session of psychodynamic psychotherapy, a distressed young woman says she dreamed she was sexually abused by her father. What do you do?

options.text: Acknowledge her distress and ask if she was abused by her father
Explore the feelings it arouses in you
Ignore the comment and continue with the flow the patient's talk
Leave it to the next session
Acknowledge her distress and ask her to talk about the dream

correct_answer.text: Acknowledge her distress and ask her to talk about the dream

correct_answers.text: Acknowledge her distress and ask her to talk about the dream

questions.explanation: Acknowledging distress is an important aspect of therapeutic relationship across varying modalities of therapy.

questions.question_text: Informal caregivers of people with a mental illness are at increased risk of developing depression and anxiety. Which of the following interventions has been shown to be the most effective in improving the mental health of caregivers?
questions.explanation: The evidence has shown that several interventions improve the mental health of caregivers. Manualised interventions - of a duration of 8 weeks or greater - with active participation are most effective. Ref: Hansen NH et al. The effect of mental health interventions on psychological distress for informal caregivers of people with mental illness: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Psychiatry. 2022;13.

questions.question_text: Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) was initially developed as a treatment for
questions.explanation: Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) uses voluntary multi-saccadic eye movements to reduce anxiety associated with disturbing thoughts and to help process emotions associated with traumatic experiences. EMDR was initially developed to help clients with PTSD. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 404-405.

questions.question_text: Which of the following refers to the parts of the collective unconscious that are pancultural representations of human experience?
questions.explanation: Carl Jung expanded on Freud's concept of the unconscious by describing the collective unconscious as consisting of all humankind's common, shared mythological and symbolic past. The collective unconscious includes archetypes (representational images and configurations with universal symbolic meanings). Archetypal figures exist for the mother, father, child, and hero, among others. Archetypes contribute to complexes, feeling-toned ideas that develop from a personal experience interacting with archetypal imagery. Thus, a mother complex is determined not only by the mother-child interaction but also by the conflict between archetypal expectation and experience with the real woman who functions in a motherly role. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1082.

questions.question_text: Interpersonal therapy has been particularly useful in the treatment of which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation: Interpersonal therapy (IPT) was developed in the 1970s by Klerman and Weissman as a treatment for depressive illness, and later developed for use in other disorders. The main indication for IPT is non-psychotic depressive disorders. Adaptations of IPT have been applied to various subgroups such as adolescents, geriatric patients, primary care clinic patients, and patients with HIV, bulimia, panic disorder, bipolar disorder, dysthymic disorder, bereavement, postpartum depression, social phobia, and insomnia. IPT is not indicated for substance abuse or personality disorders. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 914-915.

questions.question_text: According to studies by Bateman and Fonagy, mentalisation-based day hospital treatment has been shown to be superior to the standard psychiatric treatment of patients with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Treatment guidelines and meta-analyses suggest that day hospital mentalization-based treatment (MBT-DH) is a promising treatment for borderline personality disorder (BPD). In a sample of 38 BPD patients, Bateman and Fonagy compared the effectiveness of MBT-DH with that of treatment as usual (TAU; standard psychiatric care). After 18 months of treatment, MBT-DH was superior to TAU on all major outcome variables, including depressive symptoms, suicide attempts and self-harm, number of inpatients days, and social and interpersonal functioning. These results were maintained during the 18-month follow-up period up to 5 years after discharge. Ref: Laurenssen E et al. Day hospital mentalization-based treatment versus specialist treatment as usual in patients with borderline personality disorder: Randomized controlled trial. Psychological Medicine. 2018;48(15):2522-9.

questions.question_text: In which of the following therapies does positive transference get addressed early?
questions.explanation: In brief psychodynamic therapy, the therapist uses interpretation at an earlier point than in psychoanalysis. Usually there is positive transference in early sessions due to the expectation of 'magical' change. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 902-903.

questions.question_text: Which of the following predicts poor response to psychodynamic psychotherapy?

options.text: History of multiple acting out incidents

correct_answer.text: History of multiple acting out incidents

correct_answers.text: History of multiple acting out incidents

questions.explanation: Lower socioeconomic status or average IQ need not be poor predictors of response by themselves. Multiple uncontrollable 'acting out' incidents may predict recurrences and hence poor response to psychoanalysis.

questions.question_text: In psychoanalytic terms, condensation refers to

options.text: Combining several unconscious impulses into a single image while dreaming
The transfer of energy from an original object to a symbolic representation of the object
Representing abstract concepts by using recognisable images

correct_answer.text: Combining several unconscious impulses into a single image while dreaming

correct_answers.text: Combining several unconscious impulses into a single image while dreaming

questions.explanation: Condensation is the mechanism by which several unconscious wishes, impulses, or attitudes can be combined into a single image in the manifest dream content. Thus, in a child's nightmare, an attacking monster may come to represent not only the dreamer's father but may also represent some aspects of the mother and even some of the child's primitive hostile impulses as well. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1059.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a main principle of therapeutic communities?
questions.explanation: A therapeutic community is a consciously designed social environment and programme within a residential or day unit, in which the social and group process is harnessed with therapeutic intent. The main principles are democratisation, permissiveness, communalism, and reality confrontation. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 536.

questions.question_text: A middle-aged man with moderate depression is unwilling to take antidepressants but will have psychotherapy. Which factor would most make you choose brief psychodynamic therapy?

options.text: History of one previous episode of depression
Wish to know more about self

correct_answer.text: Wish to know more about self

correct_answers.text: Wish to know more about self

questions.explanation: A wish to know more about oneself, the so-called psychological mindedness and a good degree of frustration tolerance are other positive indicators to choose brief psychodynamic therapy.

questions.question_text: Mr. Z has acrophobia (fear of heights). Although he is terrified of heights, his long-term ambition in life is to become a pilot and work for the air force. Which of the interventions given below is most likely to be successful for his condition?
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) is frequently used in the treatment of phobic anxiety disorders. It is based on the behavioural principle of reciprocal inhibition (i.e. anxiety and relaxation cannot coexist). Three steps involve: 1) Relaxation training, 2) Constructing a hierarchy of anxieties, and 3) Desensitisation of the stimulus. The patient is exposed to a graded hierarchy of anxiety-provoking situations in a stepwise fashion while being taught to practice the relaxation techniques (e.g. a young woman with a spider phobia is taught relaxation techniques and then exposed to experiences starting from the lowest level of her hierarchy of anxieties - such as going to the cellar where there is the potential to come across a spider - then progressively going up the ladder to the highest - such as handling a spider). Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

questions.question_text: Transactional analysis was first developed by
questions.explanation: Eric Berne developed transactional analysis. A transaction is a stimulus presented by one person that evokes a corresponding response in another. Berne defined psychological games as stereotyped and predictable transactions that persons learn in childhood and continue to play throughout their lives. Strokes, the basic motivating factors of human behaviour, consist of specific rewards, such as approval and love. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1079.

questions.question_text: A depressed patient concludes that because he made one mistake at work, his whole career is a failure. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 911.

questions.question_text: The best treatment option for bulimia nervosa is
questions.explanation: There is more evidence for the effectiveness of eating disorder-focused CBT (CBT-ED) for bulimia nervosa than for anorexia nervosa. Individual CBT-ED is effective for adolescents as well as adults with bulimia. Treatment involves resetting dysregulated cycles of restriction-binge-purge. Intrapsychic and interpersonal skills are learned for coping with life stresses. Ref: Morris J, Anderson S. An update on eating disorders. BJPsych Advances. 2020:1-11.

questions.question_text: In the treatment of depression with a comorbid personality disorder (PD), which of the following is true?

options.text: Depressed patients with PD should receive different treatments for MDD than those without PD
Acute phase treatment outcomes for depression are worse for those with PD than without PD
Cognitive therapy (CT) is not effective for the treatment of depression with comorbid PD
Interpersonal therapy (IPT) is effective for the treatment of depression with comorbid PD
Neither CT nor IPT are effective for the treatment of depression and comorbid PD

correct_answer.text: Interpersonal therapy (IPT) is effective for the treatment of depression with comorbid PD

correct_answers.text: Interpersonal therapy (IPT) is effective for the treatment of depression with comorbid PD

questions.explanation: Depressed patients with a comorbid personality disorder (PD) should receive evidence-based treatments following guidelines for their MDD; their acute phase treatment outcome appears not worse than that of individuals with MDD without comorbid PD. Recent studies have found no impact on the effectiveness and treatment retention of cognitive therapy (CT) and interpersonal therapy (IPT) for MDD during treatment and follow-up. Depressed individuals with or without comorbid cluster C PD have been shown to benefit equally from both of these evidence-based psychotherapies. Ref: van Bronswijk SC et al. Effectiveness of acute-phase treatment of depression is not influenced by comorbid personality disorders: results from a meta-analysis and meta-regression. Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics. 2020 Mar;89(2):109. van Bronswijk SC et al. The impact of personality disorder pathology on the effectiveness of cognitive therapy and interpersonal psychotherapy for major depressive disorder. Journal of affective disorders. 2018 Jan 1;225:530-8.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not an indication for cognitive behavioural therapy?
questions.explanation: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is indicated for mild to moderate depressive illness, eating disorders, anxiety disorders (including GAD), bipolar disorder (to reduce the risk of relapse), substance use disorders, schizophrenia and other chronic psychotic disorders (as an adjunct to pharmacotherapy, for both positive and negative symptoms), and chronic medical conditions (such as fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue, and chronic pain, where there may be a psychological component and misinterpretation of physiological phenomena). Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 912. DeMartini J et al. Generalized anxiety disorder. Annals of internal medicine. 2019 Apr 2;170(7):ITC49-64.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a cognitive distortion?
questions.explanation: Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 911.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a central tenet of humanistic psychotherapy?
questions.explanation: Humanistic psychotherapy is a broad classification that embraces a diverse ensemble of approaches, assisting people to grapple with and become more of who they aspire to become. Humanistic therapy emphasises the significance of the therapeutic relationship, within which not just symptoms but complex life issues can be explored and addressed. According to Carl Rogers, there are three facilitative conditions necessary for optimal therapy: the therapist's warmth or caring; the degree to which the therapist is congruent or genuine; and the degree to which the therapist communicates unconditional positive regard for the client. Rogers and his successors have undertaken a series of quantitative investigations of client-centered therapies, finding (1) robust support for therapist relationship factors (e.g., empathy, warmth, and genuineness) over therapist technical offerings (e.g., skilled interpretations), and (2) support for client agency, as opposed to therapist directiveness, as central to successful therapeutic outcome. Schneider, KJ, Leitner, LM (2017). Humanistic Psychotherapy ☆. Reference Module in Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Psychology. pp. 1-7.

questions.question_text: A couple experienced a head-on collision while travelling in their car and escaped with less than serious injuries. Since then, the husband has not wanted to discuss the collision but suffers from repeated nightmares and flashbacks. He has stopped going to work. His wife is pursuing insurance claims against the other driver. Which of the following is most likely to be a suitable treatment for the husband?
questions.explanation: Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) uses voluntary multi-saccadic eye movements to reduce anxiety associated with disturbing thoughts and to help process emotions associated with traumatic experiences. EMDR was initially developed to help clients with PTSD. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 404-405.

questions.question_text: A 19-year-old woman has a long-standing history of self-harm, taking small overdoses and cutting herself. She is impulsive, has low self-esteem, and has constant fears of abandonment. She also has a history of sexual abuse at the hands of her stepfather. Which mode of treatment is best recommended for this patient?
questions.explanation: Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) was introduced in 1991 by Linehan and colleagues as a treatment for borderline personality disorder (BPD). Patients with BPD are supported in understanding their own emotional experiences and are taught new skills for dealing with their distress through a combination of group and individual therapy sessions. DBT is a complex treatment combining CBT interventions with Eastern meditative practice, notably mindfulness. DBT takes a hierarchical view of treatment aspirations, with the focus first on reducing behaviours that cause self-harm, then on reducing those behaviours that interfere with therapy, and finally aiming to reduce behaviours that diminish the quality of life and personal relationships. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 916-917.

questions.question_text: Availability of the therapist for telephone contact between appointments is one of the techniques used in
questions.explanation: Telephone contact is one of the techniques used in dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT). Phone contact takes place according to the contract agreed between the patient and therapist, to support the patient in applying DBT skills in real-life situations between sessions and to find alternatives to self-harming. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 917.

questions.question_text: Carl Rogers is associated with
questions.explanation: Carl Rogers developed client-centered psychotherapy, in which therapists attempt to produce an atmosphere where clients can reconstruct their strivings for self-actualisation. Therapists hold clients in unconditional positive regard, which is non-judgemental acceptance. Other therapeutic practices include attention to the present, focus on clients' feelings, emphasis on process, trust in the potential and self-responsibility of clients, and a philosophy grounded in a positive attitude towards clients, rather than a preconceived structure of treatment. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1088.

questions.question_text: Reformulation, expressed in narrative and diagrammatic forms, is a key feature of
questions.explanation: Cognitive analytic therapy (CAT) is a therapy method introduced by Anthony Ryle in 1990. It aims to bring together ideas from dynamic, cognitive, and behavioural therapies by attempting to explain psychoanalytic ideas in cognitive terms. The 'three Rs' of CAT are the recognition of maladaptive behaviour and beliefs, reformulation of these (the main 'work' of therapy), and revision. The reformulation is agreed between the therapist and patient and documented in a 'psychotherapy file'. This reformulation is expressed in narrative and diagrammatic forms and considers both the past history and current problems. It is used throughout therapy to guide the active focus, to set homework, and to enable recognition of transference/countertransference. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 918.

questions.question_text: A child who is anxious about dogs is repeatedly shown a dog while comfortably sitting on his mother's lap with an ice cream. Gradually the anxiety reduces. The principle employed here is
questions.explanation: Reciprocal inhibition is the principle that anxiety and relaxation cannot coexist. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

questions.question_text: The major principles on which a therapeutic community is based include all of the following except
questions.explanation: A therapeutic community is a consciously designed social environment and programme within a residential or day unit, in which the social and group process is harnessed with therapeutic intent. The main principles are democratisation, permissiveness, communalism, and reality confrontation. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 536.

questions.question_text: Tolerating each other's expressed emotion defines which of the following principles of therapeutic communities?
questions.explanation: Rapoport identified several defining features of a therapeutic community (TC) at the Henderson Hospital. The first characteristic of TCs is 'permissiveness', meaning that members are expected to tolerate a high level of expressed emotion. For example, members may be encouraged to verbally express their anger and to be 'authentic' in their emotions. The rationale was of catharsis and to allow members to acknowledge their 'true' feelings. TCs are structured as communal living experiences with clear boundaries and rules, support for members expressing emotion, and frequent group meetings. Ref: Veale D et al. A new therapeutic community: Development of a compassion-focused and contextual behavioural environment. Clinical psychology & psychotherapy. 2015 Jul;22(4):285-303.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a main principle of therapeutic communities?
questions.explanation: A therapeutic community is a consciously designed social environment and programme within a residential or day unit, in which the social and group process is harnessed with therapeutic intent. The main principles are democratisation, permissiveness, communalism, and reality confrontation. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 536.

questions.question_text: A 40 yr old man with alcohol problems says that he has decided to quit drinking. He is ready to accept help and advice for this and acknowledges the harm caused by alcohol. Which of the following stages of change is he in?
questions.explanation: Six stages of change: (1) Precontemplation: not even considering changing behaviour; does not see the behaviour as a problem, minimizes and denies associated risks, and avoids information to the contrary (2) Contemplation: has become aware that the behaviour is a problem but is ambivalent about changing, and likely sees equal or more benefits than costs from the behaviour (3) Preparation: has made a decision to attempt change (4) Action: has implemented a plan and is changing the behaviour (5) Maintenance: maintaining gains made and attempting to improve areas of life that have been harmed (6) Relapse: return to previous behaviour, but with the possibility of gaining useful strategies to extend the maintenance period on the next attempt. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 575.

questions.question_text: Which of the following terms refers to the unconscious development of a patient's feelings, thoughts, and attitudes towards a therapist?
questions.explanation: Transference is the unconscious development, in the patient, of feelings, thoughts, attitudes, and patterns of behaviour towards the therapist, which recapitulate earlier life relationships, most usually the patient's relationships with their parents. Transference is viewed as a defence against the reality of relationships with others. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 890.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman with dysthymia feels that every around her is depressed, but she is not unhappy. What is the most likely defence mechanism?
questions.explanation: Projection is characterised by attributing one's own internal unacceptable ideas and impulses to an external target, such as another individual, and reacting accordingly to them (e.g. an angry person accuses other people of being angry). Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 892.

questions.question_text: Which of the following types of therapy have been most studied in the treatment of borderline personality disorder (BPD)?

options.text: Dialectical behaviour therapy and psychodynamic psychotherapy
Dialectical behaviour therapy and mentalisation-based treatment
Solution-focused psychotherapy and dialectical behaviour therapy

correct_answer.text: Dialectical behaviour therapy and mentalisation-based treatment

correct_answers.text: Dialectical behaviour therapy and mentalisation-based treatment

questions.explanation: In general, psychotherapy may be more effective than usual treatment in reducing BPD symptom severity, self-harm, suicide-related outcomes and depression, whilst also improving psychosocial functioning. Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) appears to be better at reducing BPD severity, self-harm, and improving psychosocial functioning compared to usual treatment and mentalisation-based treatment (MBT) appears more effective than usual treatment at reducing self-harm and suicidality. Ref: Storebø OJ, Stoffer-Winterling JM, Völlm BA, Kongerslev MT, Mattivi JT, Jørgensen MS, Faltinsen E, Todorovac A, Sales CP, Callesen HE, Lieb K. Psychological therapies for people with borderline personality disorder. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020(5).

questions.question_text: All of the following are principles of motivational interviewing except
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing (MI) is a technique used to motivate the patient to change maladaptive behaviour. The therapist relies on empathy to convey understanding, provides support by noting the patient's strengths, and explores the ambivalence and conflicting thoughts or feelings that the patient may have about change. Principles of MI include expressing empathy (not sympathy), developing discrepancy, rolling with resistance, and supporting self-efficacy and optimism. Open questioning is one of the skills that is used to explore ambivalence and elicit change talk. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 16. https://positivepsychology.com/motivational-interviewing-principles/

questions.question_text: Klein's depressive position is related to the process of learning to cope with which of the following?
questions.explanation: Melanie Klein viewed projection and introjection as the primary defensive operations in the first months of life. Infants project derivatives of the death instinct into the mother and then fear attack from the 'bad mother', a phenomenon that Klein referred to as persecutory anxiety. This anxiety is intimately associated with the paranoid-schizoid position, infants' mode of organising experience in which all aspects of infant and mother are split into good and bad elements. As the disparate views are integrated, infants become concerned that they may have harmed or destroyed the mother through the hostile and sadistic fantasies directed toward her. At this developmental point, children have arrived at the depressive position, in which the mother is viewed ambivalently as having both positive and negative aspects, and as the target of a mixture of loving and hateful feelings. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1083.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a skill taught in DBT?
questions.explanation: Group skills training in dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) includes mindfulness skills, interpersonal effectiveness skills (e.g. problem-solving, assertiveness training, communication skills), emotion modulation skills (to change distressing emotional states), and distress tolerance skills (e.g. distraction, self-soothing strategies). Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 917.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about dream work is true?

options.text: Dreams are always interpreted in psychoanalytic psychotherapy
Dream work involves the transformation of latent content into manifest content
Dream work converts the manifest content of the dream into its latent content
Primary process thinking does not occur in dreaming
Mental mechanisms involved in the psychoanalytic theory of dreams include primary elaboration

correct_answer.text: Dream work involves the transformation of latent content into manifest content

correct_answers.text: Dream work involves the transformation of latent content into manifest content

questions.explanation: Freud distinguished between two layers of dream content. The manifest content refers to what is recalled by the dreamer; the latent content involves the unconscious thoughts and wishes that threaten to awake the dreamer. Freud described the unconscious mental operations by which latent dream content is transformed into the manifest dream as the dream work. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1059.

questions.question_text: Cognitive analytic therapy was developed by which of the following therapists?
questions.explanation: Cognitive analytic therapy (CAT) is a therapy method introduced by Anthony Ryle in 1990. It aims to bring together ideas from dynamic, cognitive, and behavioural therapies by attempting to explain psychoanalytic ideas in cognitive terms. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 918.

questions.question_text: Which of the following techniques is least used in CBT?
questions.explanation: With the paradoxical therapy approach, which evolved from the work of Gregory Bateson, a therapist suggests that the patient intentionally engage in the unwanted behaviour (called the paradoxical injunction) and, for example, avoid a phobic object or perform a compulsive ritual. Although paradoxical injunctions seem to be counterintuitive, they can create new insights for some patients. They are most often used in family therapy, though may be used in individual therapy. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 762.

questions.question_text: An 18-year-old woman with a relapse of bulimia is found to have poor engagement with the treating team. The most suitable psychological therapy would be
questions.explanation: Interpersonal therapy (IPT) was developed in the 1970s by Klerman and Weissman as a treatment for depressive illness, and later developed for use in other disorders. The main indication for IPT is non-psychotic depressive disorders, but IPT is also a strongly supported evidence-based treatment for bulimia nervosa. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 914-915. Karam AM, Fitzsimmons-Craft EE, Tanofsky-Kraft M, Wilfley DE. Interpersonal psychotherapy and the treatment of eating disorders. Psychiatric Clinics. 2019 Jun 1;42(2):205-18.

questions.question_text: Of the following, choose the initial step in assessing a patient who is afraid of spiders and avoids them.
questions.explanation: Goals of assessment for psychotherapy: - Understanding what the patient expects (or wants) from therapy - Obtaining a careful history/narrative of the problem - Establishing whether the patient can form a therapeutic relationship and make use of therapy. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 884.

questions.question_text: Choose the most accurate statement about interpersonal therapy (IPT).

options.text: The focus of IPT is on social skills development
IPT attempts to explain psychoanalytic ideas in cognitive terms
The aim of IPT is to extinguish maladaptive behaviour and substitute more adaptive ones
The goal of IPT is to empower patients to make use of their own strengths
IPT focuses on the 'here and now'

correct_answer.text: IPT focuses on the 'here and now'

correct_answers.text: IPT focuses on the 'here and now'

questions.explanation: Interpersonal therapy (IPT) was developed in the 1970s by Klerman and Weissman as a treatment for depressive illness, and later developed for use in other disorders. The rationale for IPT is that emotional disturbance (e.g. depression) tends to be associated with 'here and now' deficits in interpersonal functioning. Emotional problems are best understood by studying the interpersonal context in which they arise. Life events related to illness development include grief, interpersonal disputes, change of role, and interpersonal deficits. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 914.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a technique used in psychoanalytic psychotherapy?
questions.explanation: Psychoanalysis typically features traditional techniques to attempt to interpret unconscious content, including the 'fundamental rule' of free association, analysis of the transference/countertransference, the interpretation of dreams and 'parapraxes', and the symbolism of neurotic symptoms. Reinforcement (positive or negative) is a behavioural technique used to increase the frequency of a desired behaviour. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 898, 907.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a relative contraindication to brief time-limited psychotherapeutic approach?

options.text: Having simple and specific problems to be addressed
Good ability to form trusting relationships

questions.explanation: Chronic maladaptive patterns tend to be deeply wired and need longer therapies.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is contraindication for psychoanalytic psychotherapy?

options.text: Ability to form and sustain relationships

questions.explanation: The absence of suffering, poor impulse control, inability to tolerate frustration and anxiety, and low motivation are all contraindications for psychoanalytic psychotherapy. The presence of extreme dishonesty or antisocial personality disorder contradicts analytic treatment. Concrete thinking or the absence of psychological mindedness is another contraindication. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 745.

questions.question_text: What predicts a poor response to psychodynamic psychotherapy?

options.text: Good impulse control and good frustration tolerance
Patient can understand things in psychological terms

questions.explanation: Repeated uncontrolled self-harm can interfere significantly with the psychotherapy. In general, such patients are not suitable for a psychodynamic approach.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a cognitive technique used in CBT?
questions.explanation: Socratic questioning is a cognitive technique used in CBT to elicit further thoughts. For example, 'If that were true, what would it mean?... and what would that mean?...etc.' Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 913.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not an area of focus in interpersonal therapy (IPT)?
questions.explanation: Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 914-915.

questions.question_text: Unconditional positive regard is a feature of
questions.explanation: Carl Rogers developed client-centered psychotherapy, in which therapists attempt to produce an atmosphere where clients can reconstruct their strivings for self-actualisation. Therapists hold clients in unconditional positive regard, which is non-judgemental acceptance. Other therapeutic practices include attention to the present, focus on clients' feelings, emphasis on process, trust in the potential and self-responsibility of clients, and a philosophy grounded in a positive attitude towards clients, rather than a preconceived structure of treatment. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1088.

questions.question_text: Which of the following therapies uses 'mindfulness' as a therapeutic strategy?
questions.explanation: Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) was introduced in 1991 by Linehan and colleagues as a treatment for borderline personality disorder (BPD). Patients with BPD are supported in understanding their own emotional experiences and are taught new skills for dealing with their distress through a combination of group and individual therapy sessions. DBT is a complex treatment combining CBT interventions with Eastern meditative practice, notably mindfulness. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 916-917.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a self-rated scale?
questions.explanation: The Beck depression inventory is a self-rated questionnaire that contains 21 statements, with four possible responses for each. A total score of >17 indicates moderate depression and >30 indicates severe depression. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 97.

questions.question_text: In the management of chronic fatigue syndrome, dividing symptom-producing activities into smaller parts with interspersed rest intervals is referred to as
questions.explanation: In the management of chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS), medical providers can teach patients how to recognise their own personal energy limits and use 'pacing' (dividing symptom-producing activities into smaller parts with interspersed rest intervals) to stay within these limits. Once pacing is effectively used, some patients may be able to increase available energy and functioning, while avoiding post-exertional worsening. Of note, though CBT and graded exercise therapy (GET) have been previously recommended for CFS, the trials have been widely criticized for several design issues. Many patients have since reported that CBT and GET have not only fallen short of delivering significant improvements but have also led to worsened healthy due to ill-advised activity and exercise prescriptions. Ref: Friedberg F et al. Rethinking the Standard of Care for Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome. Journal of general internal medicine. 2020 Mar;35(3):906-9.

questions.question_text: Defence mechanisms are a function of the
questions.explanation: Defence mechanisms are a function of the ego. At each phase of libidinal development, specific drive components evoke characteristic ego defences. Defences can be grouped hierarchically according to the relative degree of maturity associated with them. Mental disorder can be characterised by the persistence of primitive defence mechanisms, with immature defences seen in early childhood, mental illnesses, and personality disturbances. Neurotic defences are seen in older children or adults experiencing stress or anxiety. Mature defences are seen in functioning adults. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1065. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 891.
